beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here is the ask, rebuilt for the camera: take a design document about a hooded runner, two gaps, a spike field, unlimited retries and a branching last zone, and hand me a playable Godot project. That prompt is an illustrative reconstruction, not a saved transcript. What sits underneath it is real — a student extension of Walker Jumpman — and we are going to play all of it.

beats.narration_text: Verdict. Everything the level claims to do, it does: the movement model, both forgiveness windows on tick evidence, both deaths and the cheap retry, pause, menu, completion, replay — and both routes completable, eleven point three and twelve point three seconds under scripted input. One defect we found on screen: the progress bar still divides by the old nine-sixty level, so it fills up around x nine sixteen and then lies for the rest of the run. Untested: nobody outside the author has played this, so whether a stranger finds the eastern climb is an open question. And cherries, moving platforms and audio are design document only. Not built — and the slice does not pretend otherwise.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here is the prompt — read it with me. 'Use Walker on my Godot platformer: replace the route fixture's right-only driver with one that takes a timed axis sequence, then generate and verify a fixture that drives the ground route's backtrack. Prove it by failing when I weaken jump velocity.' That last sentence is the whole point. A fixture that can only ever pass tells you nothing; one you can break on demand is evidence. This project's ground route is verified by a human and by a simulator, but not by a test — and that is the gap worth closing. Liam, in for Bear.
